questions.question: A TypeScript build fails — any-takeover, missing generics, or an unsound assertion: what's the diagnosis playbook?
questions.title: Ts Failure Playbook
questions.direct_answer: The failure classes with their signatures and fixes: (1) ANY-TAKEOVER — an untyped import or catch(err: any) widens everything it touches (any is CONTAGIOUS: property access on any is any, so one any at a boundary spreads through the call graph): fix by typing the BOUNDARY (unknown for catch and API responses — unknown forces narrowing; the fetch → parse → validate pipeline: response.json() as the honest unknown, then a validator/type-guard narrowing to the domain type). (2) LOST GENERICS — a function returns the SUPERTYPE because T was declared without connection or a library call erased it (useState([]) infers never[]): fix by passing the type argument explicitly (useState<User[]>([])) and structuring the generic to CONNECT positions. (3) ASSERTION ABUSE — as casts silencing a real mismatch (as User on data that isn't — the lie the compiler can't see; the unsoundness that ships to production): fix by replacing assertions with guards (is User type predicate: function isUser(v: unknown): v is User), reserving as for the honest cases (DOM refs, migrations). (4) NULL-CHECK WARS — strictNullChecks errors at scale = the migration moment: fix with nullish operators, optional chaining, and the 'make absence explicit' rule (T | null vs T with undefined).

Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    ERR[TS build failure] --> C{class}
    C -->|any spreading| A1[find the boundary: catch json untyped import]
    A1 --> A2[unknown + guard narrowing — noImplicitAny]
    C -->|never or supertype| G1[lost generic]
    G1 --> G2[explicit type argument; connect the positions]
    C -->|runtime shape crash| S1[assertion lied]
    S1 --> S2[replace as with v is guards; satisfies for validation]
    C -->|null undefined errors| N1[null-check migration]
    N1 --> N2[explicit unions, ?, ??, discriminated state]
    LADDER[complaint ladder: fix type > guard > satisfies > as last rung]
    EXP['@ts-expect-error self-tests — not a fix]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why as is unsound BY DESIGN (the model that explains the whole category): a cast is a compiler-time promise with NO runtime check — the type checker optimistically trusts you, and the mismatch surfaces at runtime exactly where JavaScript would have surfaced it (undefined property access, not a type error). Guards flip that: 'v is User' is a CHECK the compiler trusts because the predicate function executed at RUNTIME — the narrow is earned by evidence. The boundary principle follows: casts may be honest where YOU control reality (a DOM lookup you just made); they're dishonest at trust boundaries (network, storage, user input) — where validators (a tiny isUser, or a schema library — zod/valibot generate the TS type FROM the validator: type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema> — the type and the check can never drift) belong.

The inference-mechanics layer (why generics get 'lost'): TS infers T from ARGUMENTS and contextual positions — useState([]) gives the empty array NOTHING to infer from (never[]); a function whose T appears only in the RETURN can't infer (it's the phantom position); and widening rules (let x = 'hi' → string; const x = 'hi' → 'hi' — the const-assertion control: as const for readonly literal inference). The fix patterns: explicit type arguments at the low-information call site; generic parameter DEFAULTS (T = User) for the heavily-defaulted case; and satisfies preserving literals where an annotation would widen them.

The ecosystem-level answers (the senior close): type coverage tools (type-coverage % — the metric for any-contagion debt); strictness migration as a flag-by-flag program (noImplicitAny → strictNullChecks → the rest — each converts an error class into compile-time); module augmentation and declaration merging for typing the untyped dependency ONCE (a local .d.ts instead of per-call-site suppressions); and the runtime-boundary rule of thumb: TypeScript validates YOUR graph at compile time and NOTHING at runtime — every trust boundary still needs a validator (the as-response bug is this rule violated; the zod-infer pipeline is this rule obeyed — and the drift-proofing between type and validator is the payoff worth naming).
